title: System Shutdown/Reboot
summary: System Shutdown/Reboot covers deliberate attempts to power down or restart a host so that access to it is interrupted or a destructive change takes effect. The mechanism is ordinary administration turned against the owner: the built in shutdown and reboot utilities of Windows and Linux, restart or reload commands issued to a network device over a command line interface, and start, stop or reset operations sent to a hypervisor or cloud console for a virtual machine. Attackers may also call documented Windows interfaces such as InitializeSystemShutdownExW or ExitWindowsEx, and some campaigns raise a hard error to force a crash screen, which needs a privilege such as the shutdown privilege that is normally held by administrators. The visible artefacts are shutdown and restart records in the operating system event log, a matching gap in other logs, unexpected reboots in hypervisor or cloud audit trails, and configuration changes on network devices. The hard part for a defender is separating hostile restarts from the constant stream of patching, maintenance and scheduled restart activity, so the useful signal is context: an unplanned reboot immediately after disk damage, backup deletion or account changes is very different from one inside a published maintenance window.

beginner.definition: This technique is the act of turning a computer off or restarting it on purpose. An attacker does this to stop people from using the machine. It can also be done to make another harmful change take effect.
beginner.whyItMatters: A machine that is off cannot be used, so this attack damages availability. It can also hide other damage, because staff cannot look at a system that will not start. When a restart follows a disk wipe, the data may be gone for good. Some machines fail to start again at all.
howItWorks: The attacker first gets rights on a host or on the account that manages the device. These rights let them ask for a restart.
They then send a shutdown or restart command. On Windows and Linux this can be a normal built in system tool.
The same effect can be reached on network devices, where a restart or reload command runs over a command line link.
Cloud and virtual machines can be stopped, reset or deleted from a management page or a command line tool.
Some software reaches deeper interfaces and forces a crash screen instead of a clean stop. This needs extra privilege.
Attackers often restart a machine only after wiping data or breaking backups, so users cannot undo the damage.
beginner.example: Picture a hospital night desk. A worker quietly swaps the master key sheet and then pulls the building power switch. Every ward door locks at once, so nurses cannot reach patients and cannot open the record cupboard to see what changed. The switch itself is a plain, normal fitting that staff use during repairs. Only the timing tells you it was not maintenance.
takeaways: Turning a system off is an availability attack, and it can also destroy the evidence responders need.
Log the person, the time and the reason for every planned restart, so odd ones stand out.
Treat an unplanned restart after data damage as an emergency, not routine maintenance.

objectives: Explain how a shutdown or restart order reaches a host, a network device or a virtual machine.
List the log sources that record a restart and describe how a normal maintenance reboot looks in them.
Describe why attackers combine a restart with disk wiping or destroyed backups.
Recognise the warning signs of an unexpected reboot in a hypervisor or cloud audit trail.
Explain what the Windows shutdown privilege gives an attacker and who normally holds it.
